title: The Book of Songs (Shijing)
creator: shijing-poets
location: Zhou-dynasty China; compiled c. 6th century BC
note: China's oldest poetry anthology: 305 folk songs, court odes and temple hymns, later a Confucian classic.
description: The Shijing collects 305 poems in three sections: the 'Airs of the States' (Guofeng), 160 songs mostly about love, marriage, farming, war service and complaint from fifteen regions; the 'Elegantiae' (Ya), court poems of feasting and history; and the 'Hymns' (Song), sacrificial songs for the Zhou and Shang royal ancestors. Most are in rhymed four-character lines with refrains, and many open with a natural image, such as calling ospreys on a river islet, that sets the emotional key. Probably compiled by court musicians around the sixth century BC and quoted by Confucius, who said the collection could be summed up as having no twisted thoughts, it was canonised under the Han as one of the Five Classics and read through heavy allegorical commentary, the 'Mao' tradition, that made love songs into political lessons. Studied by every educated person in East Asia until the twentieth century, it also became a model for later poets seeking simplicity, and modern scholars from Marcel Granet to Wen Yiduo rediscovered its folk roots.

title: Songs of Chu (Chuci)
creator: qu-yuan
location: State of Chu; compiled by Wang Yi, 2nd century AD
note: Anthology of southern poems of shamanic journeys and exile, centred on works attributed to Qu Yuan.
description: The Chuci is the second great source of Chinese poetry. Compiled in its present form by the Han scholar Wang Yi around AD 120, it gathers poems traditionally ascribed to Qu Yuan, his follower Song Yu and later Han imitators. Unlike the northern Shijing, its poems use long lines with the exclamatory particle xi, a rich vocabulary of fragrant plants and southern place names, and the imagery of shamans who summon gods and travel through the heavens. Besides the Li Sao, it contains the Nine Songs, hymns to deities of the Chu religion; the Heavenly Questions, a sequence of riddling questions about cosmology and history; and the Summons of the Soul, which calls a dead or dying spirit back from the horrors of the four directions. The anthology gave Chinese literature its language of lament and political frustration, and was the direct ancestor of the Han rhapsody.

title: Encountering Sorrow (Li Sao)
creator: qu-yuan
note: The great lament of a rejected minister who journeys through heaven in search of a worthy ruler.
description: At about 370 lines, the Li Sao is the longest poem of early China. Its speaker announces his divine descent and noble name, describes how he adorned himself with fragrant herbs as a sign of virtue, and laments that his lord has listened to slanderers and rejected him. Unable to find understanding on earth, he rides a chariot drawn by dragons and phoenixes across the sky, seeks goddesses as brides through unreliable go-betweens, and consults shamans, before resolving to depart, only to look down on his homeland and refuse to leave. A closing envoi says he will follow the example of Peng Xian, interpreted as suicide by drowning. Traditionally read as Qu Yuan's autobiography, the poem's mix of political allegory, mythology and personal integrity created the archetype of the misunderstood loyal official, and its title became a term for any expression of grief over injustice.

title: Rhapsody on the Shanglin Park
creator: sima-xiangru
note: The most famous Han fu, a dazzling verbal panorama of Emperor Wu's hunting park.
description: This rhapsody continues Sima Xiangru's earlier Rhapsody of Sir Vacuous (Zixu fu): two fictional envoys from the states of Chu and Qi boast of their kings' hunting grounds, until a third speaker, Lord No-such, silences them by describing the emperor's Shanglin Park near Chang'an. Its rivers, mountains, rare beasts, trees, palaces and the emperor's great hunt are evoked in cascades of rhymed lines heavy with obscure binomes and ornate characters, some apparently coined for sound. At its climax the emperor, sated with pleasure, repents of extravagance, opens the park to the people and turns to Confucian virtue. Emperor Wu was so delighted that he appointed the author to court. The work epitomises the grand epideictic fu, which the critic Yang Xiong later condemned for encouraging the very excess it claimed to criticise, but it shaped Chinese literary description for centuries.

title: Nineteen Old Poems
creator: yuefu-poets
location: Eastern Han China; collected in the Wenxuan, c. 530
note: Anonymous late Han poems on parting and mortality that founded classical five-character verse.
description: The Nineteen Old Poems were grouped together in the sixth-century anthology Wenxuan, which presented them as anonymous works of the Han. Each is a short lyric in five-character lines, spoken by a traveller far from home, an abandoned wife, a drinker contemplating graves outside the city gate, or a lover separated from a beloved as the Herd Boy and Weaver Girl stars are separated by the Milky Way. Their language is simple and their emotions universal: the shortness of life, the indifference of time, the urge to seize pleasure. Critics such as Liu Xie and Zhong Rong ranked them the crown of five-character poetry, and they became a model for Cao Zhi, Tao Yuanming and the Tang poets.

title: The Peacock Flies Southeast
creator: yuefu-poets
location: Lujiang commandery (Anhui); recorded in Yutai xinyong, 6th century
note: The longest early Chinese narrative poem: a tragic tale of a young couple parted by a tyrannical mother-in-law.
description: Also known as 'A Poem Written for the Wife of Jiao Zhongqing', this anonymous ballad of over 350 five-character lines is set at the end of the Han dynasty. Liu Lanzhi, a skilled and dutiful wife, is driven out of her home by her husband's mother. The couple vow to be faithful, but her own family forces her to agree to a new marriage; on the wedding night she drowns herself, and her husband hangs himself in the courtyard. They are buried together, and a pair of birds sings over their graves. With vivid dialogue, repetition and set descriptions of clothing and weddings, the poem shows the oral techniques of yuefu at their most developed, and its criticism of family authority made it popular in modern China, where it has been adapted for opera and film.

title: The Ballad of Mulan
creator: yuefu-poets
location: Northern Dynasties China; recorded in Yuefu shiji, 12th century
note: Ballad of a young woman who takes her father's place in the army, disguised as a man.
description: The Ballad of Mulan dates probably from the Northern Wei period and survives in Guo Maoqian's twelfth-century anthology of yuefu. It opens with Mulan sighing at her loom: the emperor has called up troops and her aged father's name is on the list. She buys a horse and equipment in the markets, rides north to the Yellow River and the Black Mountains, and fights for twelve years without her comrades discovering her sex. Offered high office, she asks only for a fast camel to take her home, where she changes back into her old clothes, astonishing her fellow soldiers. The ballad ends with an image of two rabbits running side by side, impossible to tell apart. Its brisk, repetitive style and celebration of filial devotion have made Mulan a heroine of drama, opera and film throughout China and beyond.

title: Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luo River
creator: cao-zhi
note: Cao Zhi's vision of a river goddess, unattainable and longed for.
description: In his preface Cao Zhi says that, returning from the capital, he rested by the Luo River and recalled the ancient story of its goddess, Fufei. The rhapsody describes how he glimpses a woman of supernatural beauty on the riverbank; he praises her in a famous catalogue of comparisons, sends her a jade pendant as a pledge, and she responds, but he hesitates in doubt, and she withdraws with her divine retinue, sorrowing that the paths of gods and men are different. He remains, pining, through the night. Later legend read the poem as an expression of his love for his brother's empress, Lady Zhen, a story most scholars reject; others see it as political allegory. Its lyrical fusion of longing and loss made it one of the most loved fu, and it was famously painted in a scroll attributed to Gu Kaizhi and copied in calligraphy by Wang Xianzhi.

title: Peach Blossom Spring
creator: tao-yuanming
location: Xunyang, Eastern Jin / Liu Song China
note: A fisherman finds a hidden valley whose people have lived in peace, unaware of history, for centuries.
description: Tao Yuanming's short prose record, accompanied by a poem, tells how a fisherman of Wuling, following a stream lined with blossoming peach trees, passes through a narrow cave into a fertile valley of farms, ponds and mulberry trees. Its people, descendants of refugees from the Qin wars, welcome him and ask about the outside world; they know nothing of the Han or the Wei and Jin dynasties. On leaving, he marks his route and reports to the governor, but the valley can never be found again. Written in plain, calm prose, the tale offers a Daoist and agrarian utopia outside the violence of politics, and 'Peach Blossom Spring' became a lasting East Asian name for an earthly paradise, painted and versified by countless artists from Wang Wei to the Korean painter An Gyeon.

title: Returning Home
creator: tao-yuanming
note: Tao Yuanming's joyful farewell to office as he returns to his fields.
description: Tao Yuanming wrote this short rhapsody after resigning as magistrate of Pengze late in 405, with a preface explaining that he had taken the post out of poverty but could not bear to bend against his nature. The poem opens with the exclamation of its title, urging himself home since his fields and garden are growing wild, and describes the boat ride, his children and servants at the gate, the three paths overgrown with weeds but the pines and chrysanthemums still there, wine waiting in a jar. He resolves to break off social relations, climb the eastern hill, write poems by the clear stream and accept whatever fate brings. The piece became the classic statement of eremitic retirement, endlessly quoted, copied in calligraphy and painted.

title: Drinking Wine
creator: tao-yuanming
note: Twenty poems written while drinking, including the famous scene of picking chrysanthemums by the eastern hedge.
description: In a preface Tao says that, living idly with little to please him and long autumn nights, he wrote these twenty poems whenever he had been drinking alone. They range over history, friendship, poverty and the folly of officials, but the best known is the fifth, in which he builds his hut among other people yet hears no noise of carriages, because a distant mind makes its place remote; picking chrysanthemums by the eastern hedge, he sees the southern mountain, and the birds returning together at dusk hold a meaning that he cannot put into words. This poem, with its quiet blend of daily life and insight, came to embody Tao's ideal and was much admired by Su Shi and later Zen-influenced readers.

title: Climbing the Tower by the Pond
creator: xie-lingyun
note: Xie Lingyun's poem of convalescence and spring, with a celebrated couplet on pond grasses.
description: Written while Xie served unhappily as governor of Yongjia, after his demotion from court, the poem begins by contrasting the dragon hidden in the depths and the high-flying goose, images of the recluse and the official, with his own failure to be either. Bedridden through the winter, he finally opens the window and climbs the tower, seeing the changed season: spring grasses on the pond and the songs of birds altered among the willows. That couplet was admired as one of the most natural lines in Chinese poetry, and Xie himself reportedly said it came to him in a dream. The poem ends by resolving that retirement need not wait for old age. It shows his typical structure of narrative, landscape and reflection in parallel couplets.

title: Quiet Night Thought
creator: li-bai
note: Four lines on moonlight and homesickness, probably the best-known poem in China.
description: In just twenty characters, the speaker sees moonlight before his bed and mistakes it for frost on the ground; raising his head he looks at the bright moon, lowering it he thinks of his home. Traditionally said to have been written when the young Li Bai was travelling in Yangzhou, the poem uses the simplest possible vocabulary and the parallel movement of looking up and looking down to capture the experience of being far from home. Its common modern text differs slightly from the earliest versions, which speak of 'mountain moon' and 'moon's light'; the familiar wording was standardised in Ming anthologies. Learned by virtually every Chinese child, it is a touchstone of the moon as a symbol shared by people far apart.

title: Drinking Alone by Moonlight
creator: li-bai
note: Li Bai invites the moon and his shadow to drink with him, making a party of three.
description: The first of four poems with this title is among Li Bai's most loved. Among the flowers with a jug of wine and no companion, the poet raises his cup to the moon and, with his own shadow, finds himself in company of three. The moon does not drink and the shadow only follows him, but for the time being they will make merry while spring lasts: he sings and the moon lingers, he dances and the shadow sways; when drunk they will part, and he vows to meet them again far off in the Milky Way. The poem combines loneliness, humour and Daoist fantasy, turning solitude into cosmic companionship. It was probably written during his unhappy years at court, and has been translated into Western languages more often than almost any other Chinese poem.

title: Bring in the Wine
creator: li-bai
note: An exuberant drinking song urging friends to drink, since life is short and fortune comes and goes.
description: Written on an old yuefu title, this ballad opens with two famous images: the Yellow River pouring from the sky to the sea, never to return, and a mirror in a high hall showing black hair turned white in a day. The poet urges his friends Cen and Danqiu to drink deeply, declaring that heaven gave him talent for a purpose and that a thousand pieces of silver spent will come back. He dismisses sages as forgotten while only drinkers leave a name, and offers to pawn his fine horse and fur coat for more wine to drown the sorrows of ten thousand ages. Its swinging irregular lines, hyperbole and defiant joy make it the classic expression of Li Bai's persona, and it is still recited and sung.

title: The Road to Shu Is Hard
creator: li-bai
note: A wild, irregular ballad on the perilous mountain roads into Sichuan.
description: Using an old yuefu title, Li Bai evokes the legendary origins of the road from the Qin plains into Shu (Sichuan), built when heroes died hauling at the mountains, and the plank roads, cliffs, gibbering gibbons and plunging torrents that make it harder than climbing to the blue sky, a refrain that recurs throughout. Lines of three to eleven characters break all regular patterns, matching the terrain. The poem may warn a friend about the journey, or the dangers of rebellious governors in Shu; its purpose is debated. When the elder poet He Zhizhang read it in Chang'an, he reportedly called Li Bai a banished immortal, the name that stuck to him.

title: Spring View
creator: du-fu
note: Du Fu's lament in the captured capital: the nation is broken, but mountains and rivers remain.
description: Written in the spring of 757, when Du Fu was held in Chang'an after the city had fallen to An Lushan's rebels, this eight-line regulated poem opens with a celebrated antithesis: the state is shattered, yet mountains and rivers endure; in the city spring comes, and grass and trees grow thick. Flowers seem to shed tears and birds startle the heart at the sorrow of parting. War beacons have burned for three months, and a letter from home would be worth ten thousand pieces of gold. The poem ends with the poet scratching his white hair, so thin that it will scarcely hold a hatpin. Its tight parallelism and fusion of public catastrophe with private grief make it a model of Du Fu's art and one of the most memorised poems in East Asia; Bashō echoed its opening at the battlefield of Hiraizumi.

title: Ballad of the Army Carts
creator: du-fu
note: A protest against conscription and frontier wars, told through the voice of a departing soldier.
description: The poem opens with a scene on the bridge outside Chang'an: carts rumble, horses neigh, and conscripts march off with bows at their waists while parents, wives and children run alongside, crying, in a cloud of dust. A passer-by questions a soldier, who explains that men are sent to the frontier at fifteen and still serving with white hair, while fields at home lie untended. He says it is now better to bear a daughter, who can marry a neighbour, than a son who will be buried among the weeds; the poem ends with the ghosts of the dead weeping at Kokonor. Written in the new yuefu manner, directly criticising Emperor Xuanzong's expansionist wars, it established Du Fu's reputation as the poet of the people's sufferings.

title: Autumn Meditations
creator: du-fu
note: Eight linked poems recalling Chang'an from exile in the Yangtze gorges, the summit of Du Fu's late style.
description: Written at Kuizhou above the Three Gorges, where Du Fu lived in poverty and ill health, the Autumn Meditations move between the autumn landscape of the gorges, the sound of washing-stones and the poet's longing for the lost capital, recalled in increasingly dreamlike images of palaces, the Kunming Lake and the Meandering River. The eight regulated poems are linked by recurring images and form a single meditation on memory, history and the decline of the dynasty. Their dense syntax and allusive ambiguity were much admired and analysed by later critics, and they are regarded as the most complex achievement of Chinese regulated verse.

title: Wang River Collection
creator: wang-wei
location: Wang River estate, Lantian, near Chang'an
note: Twenty quatrains on scenes of Wang Wei's country estate, including the famous 'Deer Enclosure'.
description: Wang Wei and his friend Pei Di each wrote twenty five-character quatrains on twenty named spots of his estate at Wangchuan: a hill, a lake, a grove of bamboo, a magnolia enclosure. The best known, Deer Enclosure, tells of an empty mountain where no one is seen, only the echo of voices heard, and returning sunlight entering the deep wood to shine again on the green moss. The poems avoid overt emotion and the first person, letting sound, light and silence suggest a Buddhist sense of emptiness. Wang Wei is also said to have painted the estate in a handscroll, now lost but copied for centuries, so that the Wangchuan became an ideal landscape for both poets and painters.

title: Seeing Off Yuan the Second on a Mission to Anxi
creator: wang-wei
note: A farewell quatrain so loved it became the standard song of parting, the 'Weicheng Song'.
description: Wang Wei's quatrain describes the morning rain in Weicheng, west of the capital, settling the light dust, the inn green with willows (whose branches were given to departing travellers), and urges his friend, sent to the far western garrison of Anxi, to drink one more cup of wine, since west of the Yang Pass there will be no old friends. Set to music, it became known as the 'Three Refrains at Yang Pass', with the last line repeated, and was sung at farewells for centuries. It shows Wang Wei's ability to render emotion entirely through scene and gesture.

title: Song of Everlasting Sorrow
creator: bai-juyi
note: Bai Juyi's ballad of Emperor Xuanzong and Yang Guifei, from passion to catastrophe and an afterlife reunion.
description: In 120 seven-character lines, Bai Juyi tells the story of the Tang emperor Xuanzong's love for his consort Yang Guifei, which led him to neglect the state. When An Lushan's rebellion drives the court from the capital, the soldiers mutiny at Mawei and the emperor is forced to allow her death. Back in the palace after the war, he is haunted by her memory, and a Daoist adept searches heaven and earth, finding her on an island of the immortals, where she sends back keepsakes and recalls their secret vow on the seventh night of the seventh month to be birds flying wing to wing and trees with intertwined branches. The poem ends with a sorrow that will never end. Written when Bai was a young official, it was immediately popular, inspired a prose tale by Chen Hong, Yuan and Qing plays, and was beloved in Japan, where it shaped the opening of The Tale of Genji.

title: Song of the Pipa Player
creator: bai-juyi
note: On a moonlit river, the exiled poet hears a former courtesan play the pipa and tell her story.
description: Bai Juyi's preface explains that in his second year of demotion to Jiangzhou, seeing off a guest at night, he heard the sound of a pipa from a boat; the player, once a famous musician in the capital, had married a merchant who left her alone. In 88 lines the poem describes her music in a series of brilliant similes, like heavy rain and whispering, pearls falling on a jade plate, a silver vase bursting, and then her story of youthful fame and decline. The poet responds that they are both people fallen to the edge of the world, and that his blue official robe is wet with tears. Admired for its rendering of music in words and its compassion, the poem was as popular as the Song of Everlasting Sorrow.

title: New Yuefu
creator: bai-juyi
note: Fifty ballads attacking abuses of power, including 'The Old Charcoal Seller'.
description: Bai Juyi composed the fifty New Yuefu while serving as an imperial censor, declaring in his preface that they were written for the ruler, the ministers, the people, things and events, and not for literature's sake. Each poem treats a social or political problem in plain language: in The Old Charcoal Seller, an old man burns charcoal in the southern mountains and hopes the weather will stay cold, only to have his cartload seized by palace eunuchs for a length of silk; other poems describe a man who broke his own arm to avoid conscription, the oppression of taxes and the waste of court luxury. Together with Yuan Zhen's companion pieces they became the model of Chinese socially engaged poetry.

title: Discourse on Teachers
creator: han-yu
note: Han Yu's short essay defending the role of the teacher, a classic of guwen prose.
description: Written when Han Yu was teaching at the Imperial Academy, the essay argues that in ancient times learners always had teachers, whose task is to transmit the Way, impart learning and resolve doubts. Anyone who knows the Way before oneself, whatever their age or rank, is a fit teacher. Han Yu attacks the literati of his day, who are ashamed to learn from others while sending their children to masters for rote learning, and notes that even Confucius learned from many people. Written for a young follower named Li Pan, it shows the direct, argumentative and balanced style of guwen and has been studied by schoolchildren for over a thousand years.

title: Eight Records of Yongzhou
creator: liu-zongyuan
note: Eight short essays on obscure landscapes visited in exile, the founding classics of Chinese travel prose.
description: Banished to Yongzhou after the failure of the reform movement of 805, Liu Zongyuan explored the hills and streams around the town and wrote eight short accounts of his finds: the Western Hill, the Pond of Mr Gumu, the Little Rock Pool, the Yuan family ravine and others. In precise prose he describes clearing weeds, the transparency of water in which fish seem to swim in empty space, and rocks that look like animals drinking. Repeatedly he observes that these beautiful places are neglected in a remote region, an implicit parallel with his own fate. The records turned the landscape essay into an expression of the self and became models for travel writing for centuries.

title: River Snow
creator: liu-zongyuan
note: A lone fisherman in a boat on a frozen river: Liu Zongyuan's twenty-character image of solitude.
description: In four five-character lines, Liu describes a scene in which birds have vanished from a thousand mountains and human tracks from ten thousand paths; only an old man in a straw cape and hat sits in a solitary boat, fishing alone in the cold river snow. The poem is built on a progression from vast emptiness to one small figure, and the first characters of its lines have been read as a hidden message. Written in exile, it has been understood as a self-portrait of integrity in isolation. The image of the lone fisherman in snow became one of the commonest subjects of Chinese and Japanese painting.

title: The Ornamented Zither
creator: li-shangyin
note: Li Shangyin's most famous and most debated poem, on a zither of fifty strings and remembered feeling.
description: The poem begins with an ornamented zither inexplicably having fifty strings, each recalling a year of youth. Its middle couplets string together allusions: Zhuangzi dreaming he was a butterfly, the ancient king of Shu whose spirit became a cuckoo, a mermaid's tears turned to pearls in the moonlit sea, and the warm jade of Lantian giving off mist in the sun. The poem ends by saying that this feeling might have been remembered later, but even at the time it was already bewildering. Interpreters have read it as a love poem, an elegy for his wife, a preface to his collected poems or a meditation on poetry itself. Its beauty and ambiguity have made it the emblem of Li Shangyin's art.

title: Untitled Poems
creator: li-shangyin
note: A group of love poems so allusive and secretive that Li Shangyin gave them no titles.
description: About twenty of Li Shangyin's poems are titled simply 'Untitled'. They speak of secret meetings, unfulfilled longing and separation: the spring silkworm spins thread until it dies, and the candle sheds tears until it is ash; no colourful phoenix wings let lovers fly together, but their hearts are linked like the rhinoceros horn. Scholars have proposed affairs with Daoist nuns or palace ladies, or political allegories of his career, but the poems resist decoding. Their sensuous imagery, tight parallelism and refusal to explain gave Chinese poetry a new kind of private lyric, and they were imitated as the 'Xikun style' in the early Song.

title: Odes on the Red Cliff
creator: su-shi
note: Two rhapsodies on boat trips beneath the Red Cliff, meditating on history, change and the permanence of nature.
description: Exiled to Huangzhou after the poetry trial of 1079, Su Shi made two boat excursions below a cliff on the Yangtze that he took to be the site of the battle of Red Cliff (208), where Cao Cao's fleet was destroyed. In the Former Ode, written in the seventh month of 1082, a guest plays a melancholy flute and laments that even the hero Cao Cao is gone, while human life is a mayfly between heaven and earth. Su replies that, seen from the viewpoint of change, nothing lasts an instant, but from the viewpoint of constancy, we and all things are endless; the clear breeze and bright moon belong to everyone. The Latter Ode, three months later, is a mysterious winter night climb ending with a crane and a Daoist in a dream. Written in a free 'prose fu' style, the two pieces are among the most celebrated works of Chinese prose, and Su's own calligraphy of the first survives in the National Palace Museum in Taipei.

title: Remembering the Past at Red Cliff
creator: su-shi
note: Su Shi's heroic ci on the Yangtze sweeping away the heroes of the Three Kingdoms.
description: Written to the tune 'The Charms of Niannu', the lyric opens with the great river flowing east, its waves washing away the romantic heroes of a thousand ages. At the old fortress, said to be Zhou Yu's Red Cliff, rocks pierce the clouds and waves pile up like snow. Su imagines the young general Zhou Yu, newly married, with feather fan and silk turban, destroying Cao Cao's fleet amid laughter, and then mocks his own sentimental, prematurely grey self, ending by pouring a libation to the river moon, since life is like a dream. With its sweep of history and landscape it is the classic example of the 'heroic and unrestrained' ci, which Su Shi created by breaking the genre's association with love songs.

title: Prelude to Water Melody
creator: su-shi
note: A Mid-Autumn Festival lyric to the moon, written for Su Shi's absent brother.
description: Su Shi's preface says that he drank until dawn at the Mid-Autumn Festival of 1076, became very drunk and wrote this lyric thinking of his brother Su Zhe, whom he had not seen for seven years. Holding up his wine cup, he asks the moon how long it has existed and what year it is in the palaces of heaven; he wishes to ride the wind there but fears the cold, and dances with his shadow below. The second stanza turns to human separation: people have sorrow and joy, parting and reunion, as the moon waxes and wanes, and this has never been perfect; he hopes only that they may both live long and share the moon's beauty across a thousand miles. Set to music in modern times, it remains one of the most popular Chinese poems.

title: Slow Slow Tune
creator: li-qingzhao
note: Li Qingzhao's late lyric of widowhood, opening with fourteen repeated characters.
description: The lyric begins with seven pairs of reduplicated characters, a daring sequence suggesting searching, coldness, desolation and misery, unprecedented in the ci and much praised by later critics. It goes on to describe a late autumn day when the weather turns from warm to cold, a few cups of weak wine that cannot withstand the evening wind, geese flying overhead that she once recognised, chrysanthemums piled up and withered, and rain falling on the wutong tree at dusk drop by drop. The final line asks how one word, 'sorrow', could ever cover all this. Written after the loss of her husband and her home in the north, it is usually considered her masterpiece.

title: Like a Dream
creator: li-qingzhao
note: Two short early lyrics by Li Qingzhao: a boating trip among lotuses, and crabapples after a night of rain.
description: Two lyrics to the tune 'Like a Dream' are among Li Qingzhao's best-known early works. In one, she recalls a sunset at a riverside pavilion where, tipsy, she lost the way home and rowed deep into the lotus flowers, startling a flock of egrets and gulls into flight. In the other, after a night of wind and rain and heavy sleep, she asks the maid rolling up the blinds about the crabapple blossoms, is told they are unchanged, and corrects her: the leaves will be fat and the flowers thin. In a few lines each poem captures a mood with colloquial ease and visual precision, revealing the playful, observant young poet before the catastrophes of her later life.

title: Afterword to the Records on Metal and Stone
creator: li-qingzhao
note: Li Qingzhao's memoir of her marriage, book collecting and the loss of everything in war.
description: Zhao Mingcheng, Li Qingzhao's husband, compiled a catalogue of inscriptions on ancient bronzes and stones, the Jinshi lu. After his death she prepared it for publication and added an afterword that is one of the first autobiographical narratives by a Chinese woman. She recalls their early married life, when they pawned clothes to buy books and rubbings and played a game of guessing passages from the classics over tea; the growth of their collection; the flight south in 1127 with fifteen cartloads of books; Zhao's death; and the gradual loss of the remaining objects to war, theft and fraud. She ends reflecting on the vanity of possession. Its intimacy and honesty make it a classic of Chinese prose.

title: Green Jade Table: Lantern Festival
creator: xin-qiji
note: Xin Qiji's lyric of a festival night, ending with the beloved found where the lantern light is dim.
description: The lyric describes the Lantern Festival in the Southern Song capital: an east wind sets a thousand trees of fireworks blossoming at night and blows down stars like rain; jewelled carriages fill the roads, flutes sound, the jade-pot moon turns, and fish and dragon lanterns dance all night. Ladies in moth and willow ornaments pass with laughter and a trail of scent. The speaker searches the crowd a thousand times for one person, and suddenly turning his head, finds her where the lantern light is fading. The closing lines have been read as a love scene and as an image of the poet's own aloofness from the court; the scholar Wang Guowei later used them as a figure for the highest stage of learning.

title: Recalling the Past at Beigu Pavilion, Jingkou
title_native: 永遇樂·京口北固亭懷古
creator: xin-qiji
note: An old general's lament on the Yangtze, recalling past heroes and the failure to retake the north.
description: Xin Qiji wrote this lyric at sixty-five while prefect of Zhenjiang, as the court prepared an ill-judged campaign against the Jin. From the pavilion overlooking the Yangtze he remembers Sun Quan of the Three Kingdoms and Liu Yu, the fifth-century general who marched north from here, and warns of the rash Yuanjia campaign of 450 that ended in disaster. He recalls his own youth fighting in the north, forty-three years ago, and the temple to a barbarian conqueror where villagers now worship to drums. The last line asks who will inquire whether the old general Lian Po can still eat well, that is, whether the court still wants him. Dense with allusion yet passionate, it shows Xin's heroic style.

title: To My Son
creator: lu-you
note: Lu You's deathbed poem asking his son to tell him at the family sacrifice when the north is recovered.
description: In this quatrain, said to be the last poem Lu You wrote at eighty-five, he reflects that at death all things are empty, but his only grief is not to see the nine provinces united. When the imperial armies retake the central plains in the north, he asks his son not to forget to report it to him at the family sacrifice. The poem's directness and unfulfilled hope made it the most famous expression of Southern Song patriotism, and it is still taught in schools as a model of devotion to the nation.

title: The Injustice to Dou E
creator: guan-hanqing
note: A young widow wrongly executed for murder calls on heaven to prove her innocence: the most famous Chinese tragedy.
description: Dou E is sold as a child to pay her father's debts and becomes a widow while still young. A rogue, Donkey Zhang, tries to force her to marry him and poisons her mother-in-law's soup, but kills his own father by mistake. Accused, Dou E refuses to confess until the corrupt magistrate threatens to torture her mother-in-law; she is sentenced to death. On the execution ground she makes three vows: that her blood will fly up onto a white banner, that snow will fall in midsummer, and that the district will suffer three years of drought, all of which come true. Years later her ghost appears to her father, now a high official, and he rights the wrong. In four acts plus a wedge, with Dou E singing all the arias, the play combines Buddhist and Confucian ideas of karma with a sharp protest against corruption, and its full title, 'Moving Heaven and Shaking Earth', became proverbial.
image_caption: Dou E and Donkey Zhang, woodblock illustration

title: Rescuing a Fellow Courtesan
creator: guan-hanqing
note: A witty courtesan outsmarts a brutal husband to free her friend: Guan Hanqing's great comedy.
description: Song Yin-zhang, a young courtesan, ignores the warnings of her shrewd friend Zhao Pan'er and marries the rich, charming Zhou She, who begins beating her as soon as they are married. When Song sends a desperate letter, Zhao Pan'er travels to Zhengzhou, dresses up, and seduces Zhou She into promising to marry her if he divorces Song. Having obtained the divorce paper, she escapes with her friend, and when Zhou She takes them to court, the magistrate rules in the women's favour. Lively, colloquial and full of sympathy for the courtesans' resourcefulness, it is one of the masterpieces of Yuan comedy and is still performed in Chinese opera.

title: The Romance of the Western Chamber
creator: wang-shifu
note: A scholar and a minister's daughter fall in love in a Buddhist temple, helped by her clever maid Hongniang.
description: The story goes back to Yuan Zhen's Tang tale of Yingying, in which the lover abandons the heroine, and to a Jin-dynasty medley by Master Dong that gave it a happy ending. Wang Shifu's version, in an unusual twenty-one acts, tells how the young scholar Zhang Gong meets Cui Yingying in the Monastery of Universal Salvation, where she is travelling with her widowed mother. When bandits besiege the temple, the mother promises Yingying to whoever saves them; Zhang summons help, but the mother breaks her word. With the help of the maid Hongniang, who carries letters and defies her mistress, the lovers meet in secret, and Zhang finally passes the examinations and wins Yingying. Its lyrical arias and praise of love freely chosen made it immensely popular and controversial; it is the book Baoyu and Daiyu read together in Dream of the Red Chamber, and Hongniang's name became a word for a matchmaker.

image_caption: Colour woodblock illustration from Min Qiji's edition, 1640

title: Romance of the Three Kingdoms
creator: luo-guanzhong
note: Epic historical novel of the wars that followed the fall of the Han, with Liu Bei, Cao Cao and Zhuge Liang.
description: Based on Chen Shou's third-century history and centuries of storytelling and drama, the novel covers about a century from the Yellow Turban rebellion of 184 to the reunification of China under the Jin in 280. It begins with the oath of brotherhood sworn in a peach garden by Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, and follows their struggle against the cunning Cao Cao and the southern state of Wu, culminating in the battle of Red Cliff and the long campaigns of the strategist Zhuge Liang. Written in a simplified classical Chinese, it blends history with legend, about seven parts fact to three parts fiction in the traditional estimate. The standard 120-chapter version was edited by Mao Lun and Mao Zonggang around 1680. One of the Four Classic Novels, it has shaped popular ideas of loyalty, strategy and heroism across East Asia: Guan Yu became a god of war and wealth, and the story lives on in opera, comics and video games.
image_file: 新刊校正古本大字音释三国志通俗演义 明万历十九年书林周曰校刊本 002.jpg
image_caption: Page of the 1591 Zhou Yuejiao edition

title: Water Margin
creator: shi-naian
note: The adventures of 108 outlaws gathered at Liangshan Marsh, rebels against corrupt officials.
description: Water Margin grew from stories about the historical bandit Song Jiang, active around 1120 in the Northern Song. In its main versions of 100 or 120 chapters it tells how a series of heroes, each driven to outlawry by injustice, gather at the marshes of Mount Liang: the drinking tiger-slayer Wu Song, the hot-tempered monk Lu Zhishen, the drill instructor Lin Chong, the axe-wielding Li Kui and many others, until 108 chiefs are assembled under Song Jiang. They fight imperial armies, are eventually granted amnesty, and are destroyed fighting for the dynasty. Jin Shengtan's 70-chapter edition of 1641, which ends at the gathering of the heroes, was the most read version for three centuries. With its vivid colloquial language and episodes of violence and brotherhood, the novel is one of the Four Classics; it inspired Jin Ping Mei, Bakin's Hakkenden and countless ukiyo-e prints by Kuniyoshi.
image_caption: Page from an early printed edition

title: Journey to the West
creator: wu-chengen
note: The Monkey King escorts the monk Tripitaka on his pilgrimage to India in a comic fantasy of demons and gods.
description: The novel is based on the real journey of the monk Xuanzang to India in 629–645 to collect Buddhist scriptures, transformed over centuries of popular storytelling into a fantasy. Its 100 chapters begin with the birth of Sun Wukong, a monkey born from a stone, who acquires magic powers and wreaks havoc in heaven until the Buddha imprisons him under a mountain. Released to serve as disciple to the monk Tripitaka, he travels west with the greedy Pigsy, the gloomy Sandy and a dragon-horse, overcoming eighty-one ordeals posed by demons who want to eat the monk's flesh. Humorous and satirical, it mocks the celestial bureaucracy while serving as an allegory of the mind's discipline in Buddhist, Daoist and Confucian terms. One of the Four Classic Novels, it is the source of endless operas, films, cartoons and manga, including Dragon Ball.

image_caption: Illustration from the first edition, Shidetang, Nanjing, 1592

title: Jin Ping Mei
creator: lanling-xiaoxiao-sheng
note: The rise and fall of the merchant Ximen Qing and his household of wives and concubines: the first Chinese novel of domestic life.
description: Jin Ping Mei, whose title combines the names of three of its women (Golden Lotus, Vase and Plum Blossom), takes an episode from Water Margin, the adultery of Pan Jinlian and Ximen Qing, and develops it into a hundred-chapter novel. Ximen, a pharmacist turned official in a small town in Shandong, accumulates wealth, bribes officials and gathers wives and concubines, whose rivalries, schemes and pleasures fill the novel, until he dies of excess and his household disintegrates. Its graphic sexual scenes caused it to be banned repeatedly, but its realistic detail about food, clothing, money and speech, its satire and its complex structure were admired by critics such as Zhang Zhupo. Dream of the Red Chamber owes much to it.
image_caption: Woodblock illustration to chapter 17, Ming edition

title: The Peony Pavilion
creator: tang-xianzu
note: A young woman dies of longing for a man she met in a dream, and is brought back to life by love.
description: Du Liniang, the daughter of a strict prefect, falls asleep in her family's garden and dreams of a young scholar who makes love to her among the peonies. She pines away for him, paints her self-portrait and dies, and is buried in the garden. Three years later the scholar Liu Mengmei, whom she dreamed of, finds the portrait and is visited by her ghost; with the help of the judge of the underworld he opens her grave, and she returns to life. After many trials, including her father's disbelief, the emperor approves their marriage. Tang Xianzu's preface declares that love can cause death and restore life. The long kunqu play's lyrical arias and celebration of passion against Confucian propriety made it hugely influential; women readers wrote commentaries on it, and the 'Startled Dream' scene is still at the heart of the kunqu repertory.
image_caption: Ming-dynasty printed edition

title: The Peach Blossom Fan
creator: kong-shangren
note: A love story between a scholar and a courtesan set against the fall of the Ming at Nanjing.
description: The play follows the young scholar Hou Fangyu and the courtesan Li Xiangjun in Nanjing in the 1640s. Hou gives Li a fan as a token of love; when corrupt officials of the short-lived Southern Ming court try to force her to marry one of them, she resists and strikes her head, spattering the fan with blood, which a painter friend turns into a spray of peach blossoms. As the Manchu armies advance and the court collapses through factionalism, the lovers are separated and finally meet again in a Daoist temple, where a priest tears the fan and tells them that, with country and ruler gone, love is meaningless; both become recluses. Kong Shangren researched the historical events carefully, and the play's mixture of romance and political lament, its colourful minor characters such as the storyteller Liu Jingting, and its unusual unhappy ending made it the last masterpiece of chuanqi.

image_caption: Qing printed edition

title: Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio
creator: pu-songling
location: Zichuan, Shandong; first printed in Hangzhou, 1766
note: Nearly 500 classical-language tales of fox spirits, ghosts and the supernatural, sharp with social satire.
description: The Liaozhai zhiyi, literally 'Records of the Strange from the Studio of Leisure', contains some 490 pieces, from brief anecdotes to elaborate stories. In the most famous, a scholar falls in love with a beautiful woman who turns out to be a fox spirit or a ghost: in Nie Xiaoqian, a ghost girl enslaved by a demon is rescued by an upright scholar and returns to life; in The Painted Skin, a man takes home a beautiful girl who is really a demon wearing a painted human skin. Other tales mock examiners who cannot recognise talent, officials who torture the innocent, and the absurdities of daily life. Written in an allusive, compact classical prose that revived the Tang tale, the book circulated in manuscript for decades before its first printing. Its stories have been adapted into countless operas, films, such as A Chinese Ghost Story (1987), and television series.
image_caption: Illustration of the tale Nie Xiaoqian from a Qing illustrated edition

title: The Scholars
creator: wu-jingzi
note: A satirical panorama of scholars obsessed with examinations, fame and appearances.
description: Set nominally in the Ming dynasty but clearly reflecting the eighteenth century, The Scholars has no single plot; its 56 chapters pass from character to character like a scroll. Among its famous episodes, Fan Jin, an old candidate who has failed for decades, goes mad with joy on finally passing the provincial examination and is slapped back to sanity by his butcher father-in-law, who had always despised him; a stingy dying man cannot close his eyes until two lamp-wicks are reduced to one. Against these hypocrites the novel sets a few men of real integrity, including Du Shaoqing, a self-portrait of the author, and a group who rebuild a temple to an ancient sage. Its ironic understatement made it, for Lu Xun and Hu Shi, the first great Chinese satirical novel.

title: Dream of the Red Chamber
creator: cao-xueqin
location: Beijing; first printed by Cheng Weiyuan and Gao E, 1791
note: The decline of the aristocratic Jia family and the love of Jia Baoyu and Lin Daiyu: the greatest Chinese novel.
description: Also called The Story of the Stone, the novel begins with a magic stone left over when the goddess Nüwa repaired the sky, which is carried into the human world and born as Jia Baoyu, the sensitive heir of a great family in the capital, who prefers the company of girls to the study of the classics. He grows up in the Prospect Garden, built for a visit by his sister, an imperial consort, among a dozen remarkable young women, above all his frail, poetic cousin Lin Daiyu and the sensible Xue Baochai. Over 120 chapters and some 400 characters, the family's wealth and morals decay; Baoyu is tricked into marrying Baochai, Daiyu dies, and Baoyu leaves the world as a monk. Only the first 80 chapters are certainly by Cao Xueqin; the last 40 were published by Cheng Weiyuan and Gao E, perhaps using his drafts, a question long debated. Its psychological depth, poetry and detailed picture of Qing elite life make it the subject of 'Redology', a scholarly field in its own right.
image_caption: Qing-dynasty illustration of the novel

title: Six Records of a Floating Life
creator: shen-fu
note: A minor clerk's memoir of his marriage, travels and sorrows: an intimate classic of Chinese prose.
description: Shen Fu planned six chapters but only four survive: on the joys of married life, the pleasures of leisure, the sorrows of hardship and his travels. The heart of the book is his wife Chen Yun, his cousin, whom he describes with unusual tenderness: she dresses as a man to attend a festival with him, puts tea leaves in lotus flowers overnight to scent them, and plans to find him a concubine. Disapproval from his parents, debts and illness drive them from home, and Yun dies in poverty. Written with candour and charm, outside the conventions of formal literature, the memoir was discovered in manuscript in the nineteenth century and became a favourite of modern Chinese readers; Lin Yutang translated it into English.

title: A Madman's Diary
creator: lu-xun
note: A man convinced that everyone around him is a cannibal: the first modern Chinese short story.
description: Published in the May 1918 issue of New Youth, the story is framed by a short classical-Chinese preface explaining that the narrator found the diary of an old schoolfriend, since recovered from a mental illness. The diary itself, in vernacular Chinese, records the madman's growing conviction that his elder brother, his neighbours and even his doctor intend to eat him, and his discovery, reading between the lines of a history book full of words about benevolence and righteousness, the words 'eat people'. It ends with a cry to save the children. Modelled partly on Gogol's story of the same title, it was the first important work of fiction in modern vernacular Chinese, and its image of Confucian society as cannibalistic became a slogan of the New Culture movement.

title: The True Story of Ah Q
creator: lu-xun
note: A village labourer who turns every humiliation into a 'spiritual victory': Lu Xun's portrait of the national character.
description: Ah Q is a landless odd-job man in the village of Weizhuang who has no proper name, home or family. Beaten and mocked by everyone, he consoles himself by imagining that he has won, for example by thinking of his tormentors as his sons, and in turn bullies those weaker than himself. When the 1911 revolution reaches the area, he decides to join it, mainly in hope of loot and women, but the local gentry simply rename themselves revolutionaries; Ah Q is arrested for a robbery he did not commit and executed, worrying chiefly that he cannot draw a perfect circle on his confession. Serialised under a pseudonym, the story satirised the self-deception and servility Lu Xun saw in Chinese society, and 'Ah Q-ism' became an everyday term.

title: Call to Arms
creator: lu-xun
note: Lu Xun's first collection of stories, with a famous preface comparing China to an iron house.
description: Call to Arms (Nahan) collects fourteen stories written between 1918 and 1922, including A Madman's Diary, Kong Yiji, about an impoverished failed scholar mocked in a tavern, Medicine, in which a family buys a bun soaked in an executed revolutionary's blood to cure their son, My Old Home and The True Story of Ah Q. In its preface Lu Xun recalls his youth and his turn from medicine to literature, and describes a conversation in which he compared China to an iron house without windows, full of sleeping people who will suffocate; to wake a few of them would only make their death more painful, yet one cannot say there is no hope of destroying the house. The collection established modern Chinese fiction and is one of the most influential books of the twentieth century in China.

title: Wild Grass
creator: lu-xun
note: Twenty-three dark, dreamlike prose poems, Lu Xun's most personal and enigmatic work.
description: Written in 1924–26, during a period of political repression and personal crisis, the pieces of Wild Grass are prose poems influenced by Baudelaire and Turgenev. They include dream visions, allegories and dialogues: a traveller who keeps walking toward an unknown destination, a corpse that reads its own epitaph, a soldier advancing alone into a 'formation of nothingness', and a tree in a backyard. Their imagery of shadows, death and despair, and their refusal of easy hope, make them the most modernist side of Lu Xun, and they have attracted increasing critical attention since the 1980s.

title: Midnight
creator: mao-dun
note: A panorama of 1930 Shanghai: an industrialist's struggle against foreign capital, speculators and strikers.
description: The novel centres on Wu Sunfu, an ambitious silk-factory owner who dreams of building Chinese industry. Over a few months in 1930, as civil war rages, he battles the comprador financier Zhao Botao on the bond market, crushes a strike in his factory, and is finally ruined. Around him Mao Dun presents landlords fleeing peasant uprisings, decadent young intellectuals, revolutionaries and speculators. Intended as a Marxist analysis of why China could not develop an independent capitalism, it was the most ambitious realist novel of its time and remains a key work of left-wing literature.

title: Rickshaw Boy
creator: lao-she
note: A young rickshaw puller in Beijing struggles to own his own vehicle and is gradually crushed.
description: Xiangzi, a strong, honest young peasant who has come to Beijing, has one dream: to own a rickshaw. He saves for three years and buys one, only to have it seized by soldiers; he escapes with three camels, earning the nickname Camel. His savings are stolen, he is tricked into marriage by Huniu, the daughter of a rickshaw-garage owner, who dies in childbirth, and the girl he loves is sold into prostitution and kills herself. By the end Xiangzi has become a cynical, degraded loafer. Lao She's realistic, humorous and compassionate portrait of the Beijing poor, in its lively local dialect, made it a classic. A bowdlerised English translation of 1945 with a happy ending was a bestseller in America.

title: Teahouse
creator: lao-she
note: Fifty years of Chinese history seen through one Beijing teahouse and its customers.
description: Teahouse's three acts are set in the Yutai teahouse in 1898, after the failure of the Hundred Days' Reform; around 1918, in the warlord era; and in the late 1940s, under the Nationalists. Its owner, Wang Lifa, tries to adapt and survive, while dozens of characters, from Manchu bannermen and eunuchs to informers, refugees and gangsters, pass through. In the final scene three old men scatter paper money for their own funeral. Lao She's play, first staged in 1958 in a famous production by Jiao Juyin, is regarded as the masterpiece of Chinese spoken drama (huaju), and the Beijing People's Art Theatre still performs it.

title: Border Town
creator: shen-congwen
note: A girl, her grandfather and two brothers in a river town of western Hunan: Shen Congwen's pastoral masterpiece.
description: In the small town of Chadong on the border of Hunan and Sichuan, an old ferryman lives with his granddaughter Cuicui. Two brothers, sons of a local boat owner, both fall in love with her: the elder proposes through a go-between, the younger by singing love songs across the river at night. Misunderstandings, pride and silence lead to the elder brother's drowning, the younger brother's departure and the grandfather's death in a storm; Cuicui is left waiting at the ferry for someone who may or may not return. Written in a lyrical, understated style, the novella evokes a world of natural goodness and local customs, such as the Dragon Boat Festival, that Shen saw as threatened by modernity. It is among the most beloved works of modern Chinese literature.

title: Family
creator: ba-jin
note: Three brothers in a Chengdu gentry household rebel, submit or escape under their tyrannical grandfather.
description: Set in Chengdu around 1920, Family follows the brothers of the Gao household. The eldest, Juexin, gives up his studies and the cousin he loves to accept an arranged marriage and run the family business, then sees his wife die in childbirth outside the house because of superstition. The second, Juemin, defies the family to marry his cousin. The youngest, Juehui, a student inspired by the May Fourth movement, loves the maid Mingfeng, who drowns herself when she is given as a concubine to an old man, and at the end he leaves for Shanghai. The novel's indictment of the patriarchal family moved generations of young readers; it was followed by Spring and Autumn to form the Turbulent Stream trilogy.

title: Love in a Fallen City
creator: eileen-chang
note: A divorcee and a playboy play a game of love in Hong Kong until the Japanese invasion forces a decision.
description: Bai Liusu, a divorced woman humiliated by her declining Shanghai family, goes to Hong Kong with Fan Liuyuan, a wealthy, cynical overseas Chinese who wants her as a mistress, not a wife. Their elaborate courtship, a battle of wit and calculation, seems to end with her becoming a kept woman, until the Japanese attack on Hong Kong in December 1941. Amid the bombardment the two find a moment of genuine dependence, and they marry. The title plays on a classical phrase for a beauty who causes the fall of a city, inverting it: here, Chang suggests, a city fell so that one woman's marriage could be achieved. Its irony, rich imagery and understanding of women's economic constraints made it one of her most celebrated works, filmed by Ann Hui in 1984.

title: The Golden Cangue
creator: eileen-chang
note: A woman married into a wealthy family for money becomes a tyrant who destroys her own children.
description: Cao Qiqiao, the daughter of a sesame-oil shopkeeper, is married off to the invalid second son of the wealthy Jiang family, where she is despised. After years of frustration, during which she is drawn to her rakish brother-in-law Jiping, she inherits her share of the family wealth, and the 'golden cangue', the heavy wooden collar of a prisoner made of gold, closes around her. She drives off Jiping when she suspects he wants her money, and over decades destroys the lives of her son and daughter, making her son an opium addict and wrecking her daughter's engagement. Chang's psychological study of avarice and repression was praised by the critic C. T. Hsia as the greatest novella in the history of Chinese literature.

title: Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters)
creator: kojiki-compilers
note: Japan's oldest surviving book: the creation of the islands, the age of the gods and the early emperors.
description: The Kojiki, in three books, was presented to Empress Genmei in 712. The first tells of the creation: the divine pair Izanagi and Izanami give birth to the Japanese islands and many gods; Izanami dies and Izanagi pursues her to the underworld; the sun goddess Amaterasu hides in a cave after the outrages of her brother Susanoo and is lured out by a comic dance; and her grandson descends to rule the land. The second and third books narrate the legendary first emperor Jinmu and his successors down to Empress Suiko (d. 628), with tales of the hero Yamato Takeru. Written in a hybrid of Chinese and Japanese, it preserves over a hundred early songs. Its purpose was to establish the descent of the imperial house from Amaterasu. Neglected for centuries in favour of the Chinese-style Nihon shoki of 720, it was revived by Motoori Norinaga in the eighteenth century and became a sacred text of State Shinto before 1945.
image_caption: Shinpukuji manuscript of the Kojiki, 1371–72, the oldest surviving copy

title: Man'yōshū (Collection of Ten Thousand Leaves)
creator: otomo-no-yakamochi
note: The first anthology of Japanese poetry: some 4,500 poems by emperors, courtiers, soldiers and peasants.
description: The Man'yōshū contains about 4,500 poems in twenty books, dating mostly from about 600 to 759, the date of its last poem, by Ōtomo no Yakamochi, who is generally thought to have given the collection its final shape. Most are tanka of 31 syllables, but there are also some 260 chōka, long poems, the greatest of them by Kakinomoto no Hitomaro, and a few other forms. Besides court poems for imperial journeys and laments for princes, the anthology includes love poems, songs of the eastern provinces in dialect, poems by frontier guards (sakimori) leaving their families, and Yamanoue no Okura's Dialogue on Poverty. They are written in man'yōgana, Chinese characters used phonetically, a script that became the origin of the kana syllabaries. Prized from the eighteenth century by nationalist scholars as the expression of an unspoiled Japanese spirit, it is still the source of names; the era name Reiwa (2019) was taken from its preface to a group of plum-blossom poems.
image_caption: Ranshi-bon fragment, Heian-period manuscript of the Man'yōshū, Tokyo National Museum

title: Poems at Iwami on Parting from His Wife
creator: kakinomoto-no-hitomaro
note: Hitomaro's long poems on leaving his wife in Iwami, among the greatest chōka of the Man'yōshū.
description: In these paired chōka, each followed by short envoy poems (hanka), Hitomaro describes the coast of Iwami on the Sea of Japan, where seaweed sways in the waves like his wife lying beside him, and his journey inland to the capital; as he climbs, he turns to look back again and again, but the village recedes and the mountains rise between them. He begs the mountains to bow down so that he may see her gate. The poems combine the formal devices of chōka, pillow words, parallelism and accumulated imagery, with a vivid personal emotion that made them models of the form. Whether they record Hitomaro's own experience or are a court performance in a persona is debated.

title: Kokin Wakashū
creator: ki-no-tsurayuki
note: The first imperial anthology of Japanese poetry, which set the standards of court poetry for a millennium.
description: Commissioned by Emperor Daigo and compiled by Ki no Tsurayuki, Ki no Tomonori, Ōshikōchi no Mitsune and Mibu no Tadamine, the Kokinshū contains about 1,100 poems, almost all tanka, arranged in twenty books by topic: six books of the four seasons, followed by congratulations, parting, travel, names of things, five of love, laments and miscellaneous. Within each book poems are ordered to form a progression, for example from the first haze of spring to the falling of the cherry blossoms. The style is elegant, witty and reflective, rich in wordplay (kakekotoba) and personification, in contrast to the directness of the Man'yōshū. Tsurayuki's Japanese preface and Ki no Yoshimochi's Chinese preface set out the first theory of Japanese poetry. It was the first of twenty-one imperial anthologies, and its vocabulary and seasonal associations shaped all Japanese poetry, art and design until the nineteenth century.
image_caption: Gen'ei-bon manuscript of the Kokinshū, 12th century

title: Tosa Diary
creator: ki-no-tsurayuki
note: A governor's journey home by sea, written in kana in the voice of a woman in his party.
description: The diary covers fifty-five days from late 934 to early 935, as Tsurayuki returned from his governorship of Tosa on Shikoku to the capital, mostly by boat along the coast, delayed by bad weather and fear of pirates. It famously opens by saying that diaries are written by men, but a woman will try her hand at one too: by adopting a female persona Tsurayuki could write in kana rather than Chinese. The narrative records farewells, drinking parties, poems composed by passengers including children, and repeated grief for a little girl who died in Tosa. The diary's mixture of prose and waka, humour and sorrow made it the first literary diary in Japanese and opened the way for the great women's diaries of the following century. A copy made by Fujiwara no Teika survives.
image_caption: Copy of the Tosa Diary made by Fujiwara no Teika

title: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
creator: heian-anonymous-authors
note: A tiny princess found in a bamboo stalk grows up, rejects her suitors and returns to the moon.
description: An old bamboo cutter finds a tiny girl, three inches tall, glowing inside a stalk of bamboo, and he and his wife raise her. She grows within three months into a woman of radiant beauty, Kaguya-hime, and five noble suitors seek her hand; she sets each an impossible task, such as fetching the Buddha's stone begging bowl or a jewel from a dragon's neck, and they fail in comic ways. Even the emperor's love cannot keep her: she reveals that she is from the moon, and on the night of the full moon a heavenly host descends to take her back, wrapping her in a feather robe that erases her earthly feelings. She leaves the emperor an elixir of immortality, which he orders burned on the highest mountain, explaining the name of Mount Fuji. Called by Murasaki Shikibu the ancestor of all monogatari, it is Japan's oldest surviving prose tale and inspired Takahata Isao's film The Tale of the Princess Kaguya (2013).

image_caption: Illustrated Taketori monogatari, Metropolitan Museum of Art

title: The Tales of Ise
creator: heian-anonymous-authors
note: 125 short episodes built around poems, following the loves and travels of an unnamed 'man of old'.
description: Each episode of the Tales of Ise begins with the phrase 'Once there was a man' and leads to one or more waka. The episodes, many linked to poems by Ariwara no Narihira, sketch a life from coming of age to death: a secret love for a high-born lady who becomes an imperial consort, an affair with the Ise priestess, and a journey east into exile, where at the Sumida River he asks a bird about his love in the capital and, at Yatsuhashi, writes a poem whose syllables spell the name of the iris. The work grew over the tenth century and its authorship is unknown. It became the model of courtly love and elegance, one of the most commented-on texts of Japanese literature, and a favourite subject of painting, from Heian scrolls to the iris screens of Ogata Kōrin.
